catalog_quote: 5.3.2. Stress. Stress is non-contrastive and occurs as follows: Two-syllable words, always on first syllable. /ata/ ('ata) 'people' /vani/ ('pani) 'sun' /goe/ ('goɛ) 'cloud' Three-syllable words, always on second syllable. /tumanu/ (tu'manu) 'scratch' /moaga/ (mo'aga) 'many' /otogo/ (o'togo) 'sky' Four-syllable words, always on second syllable. /evudenu/ (ɛ'budɛnu) 'hold on lap' /tumuanu/ (tu'muanu) 'hurt' /bolekava/ (bo'lɛkaba) 'green python' Five-syllable words, always on second and fourth syllables. There is no recognizable difference between the two stresses. /kubilianu/ (ku'bili'anu) 'to be dull' /evutivanu/ (ɛ'buti'banu) 'mix together' /galasianu/ (ga'lazi'anu) 'dive' ... [sec. 5.1.2, ms p. 5:] Stress is not indicated emically as it is predictable. ... [sec. 4 item 4, ms p. 5:] They are both units of stress placement. The rhythmic pattern is the same in a CVVCV as in a CVCVCV pattern, that is, each is a three-syllable word with stress/pitch on the second syllable. For example: /heinu/ (xɛ'inu) 'cut' /dabanu/ (da'banu) 'cold' ... [OPD p. 2:] Stress is on first syllable in two-syllable words, on second syllable in three-, and four-syllable words, and on the second and fourth syllables of five-syllable words.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and counted from the left edge: it falls on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables, but on the first syllable of disyllables (i.e. never on the final syllable); five-syllable words carry stress on both the second and fourth syllables. Equivalent to left-to-right iambs with final-syllable non-finality. Each vowel of a vowel sequence counts as its own syllable for stress placement (sec. 4: /heinu/ [xe'inu] 'cut' patterns as a trisyllable). The OPD (c.1983/2004) restates the same rule: 'Stress is on first syllable in two-syllable words, on second syllable in three-, and four-syllable words, and on the second and fourth syllables of five-syllable words.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: In five-syllable words stress falls on both the second and fourth syllables and 'there is no recognizable difference between the two stresses' (no primary/secondary ranking given); nothing said for four-syllable words beyond the single second-syllable stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables take initial rather than second-syllable stress; no lexical exceptions mentioned; stress explicitly 'non-contrastive' and 'not indicated [phon]emically as it is predictable' (sec. 5.1). Phonetic correlates: stressed syllable slightly lengthened, final syllable slightly shortened (5.3.1); word-level pitch: first syllable level, middle syllable(s) slightly higher, final slightly lower (sec. 6).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for words in isolation (citation forms, incl. inflected verbs in -anu/-nu); rule is by syllable count of the phonological word; Efogi dialect. Note Dutton 2010:8 says stress is 'typically contrastive' across Koiarian but names MTN among the languages not described in detail; the Garlands' first-hand analysis says non-contrastive for Mountain Koiali.
new_statements.identity_note: All Garland sources describe the dialect of Efogi village (headwaters of the Brown River, Central Province), i.e. Mountain Koiali proper = Glottolog moun1252 / ISO kpx; the OPD names 'Mt Koiali Language [KPX]', major village Efogi. No sub-dialect glottocode needed.

new_statements.quote: Stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable in Biage. In Mountain Koiali, Garland and Garland state that stress is non-contrastive and always falls on the penultimate syllable with the exception of five syllable words, where the stress falls on both the second and fourth syllables (1971:15–16). He also says, “The stressed syllable is usually slightly lengthened and the final syllable is slightly shortened. Otherwise, each syllable, ie. each vowel, tends to exercise its full value” (1971:15). Retsema did not find anything in his analysis of the Biage wordlists that would contradict Garland’s rules if they are applied to Biage as well.

new_statements.relation_note: The only Mt Koiali content is a second-hand paraphrase of Garland & Garland 1971, the very source behind the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 0100 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable). The paraphrase agrees for 2-, 3- and 5-syllable words (initial = penult; second = penult; second + fourth) but states 'always.. penultimate', which for four-syllable words gives 0010 where the catalog (and Garland 1971:15-16, checked in the on-disk scanned: 'Four-syllable words, always on second syllable') has 0100. This is a summarising error in the survey, not new evidence: the survey collected no Mt Koiali data. Its own primary finding ('typically.. penultimate') is for Biage [bdf], whic…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Biage (the survey's own wordlist data): stress typically on the penultimate syllable. For Mountain Koiali the survey gives no primary data; it paraphrases Garland & Garland 1971 as: stress non-contrastive, always penultimate, except five-syllable words, which are stressed on the second and fourth syllables. The stressed syllable is slightly lengthened and the final syllable slightly shortened (quoted from Garland & Garland 1971:15).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Five-syllable words carry stress on both the second and fourth syllables (survey's restatement of Garland & Garland 1971:15-16; the 1971 ms adds 'There is no recognizable difference between the two stresses').
new_statements.exceptions: 'Typically' hedges the Biage penultimate rule; no exceptions are listed for Biage. For Mountain Koiali the only exception named is the five-syllable case (second + fourth). The survey's 'always penultimate' collapses Garland & Garland's four-syllable rule ('Four-syllable words, always on second syllable', i.e. antepenult, e.g. /evudenu/ (e'budenu) 'hold on lap', /oolekava/ (bo'lekaba) 'green python') into 'penultimate', which is not what the 1971 ms says.
new_statements.identity_note: Hiley, Gray & Retsema 2015 is a survey of Biage [bdf] (Kokoda area, Oro Province), which Dutton 1969 had treated as part of the Northern dialect of Mountain Koiari; the survey concludes (p.3) that 'Biage is a separate language from Mountain Koiali [kpx], of which it was previously considered a dialect.' Its penultimate-stress statement is about Biage; everything it says about Mountain Koiali proper is quoted or paraphrased from Garland & Garland 1971 (the Central Province, Kokoda-trail variety). The Biage statement is already logged under biag1234.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, and it is an artefact of paraphrase rather than of data. Hiley, Gray & Retsema 2015 (p.34) summarise Garland & Garland 1971 as 'stress.. always falls on the penultimate syllable with the exception of five syllable words', whereas Garland & Garland 1971 sec. 5.3.2 (ms pp.15-16, on-disk scanned) say: two-syllable words on the first syllable, three-syllable words on the second, four-syllable words on the second (antepenult, e.g. (e'budenu) 'hold on lap'), five-syllable words on the second and fourth with no recognizable difference between the two stresses. The two descriptions coincide except for four-syllable words (survey's reading 0010 vs Garland/catalog 0100). Since the survey cites Garland as its only Mt Koiali source and reports no Mt Koiali wordlist analysis, the 1971 ms (and the SIL OPD restatement) remains the description of record; the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 0100 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable) is unchanged. The survey's positive claim (penultimate) is for Biage, which it treats as a distinct language, and it notes only that nothing in the Biage wordlists contradicts Garland's rules if applied to Biage.

Sec 5.3.1: stressed syllable slightly lengthened, final syllable slightly shortened.
